#1040. Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

The big talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

“After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” said Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

It was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

“I need to praise the players,” said Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”

When it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” said Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

One last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down quickly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

Arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

This is about as dominant as Newcastle have been in a game all season but they have not been able to find a goal from some where. They have just gone close again as Will Osula just fails to reach Amar Dedic’s cross.

Arteta has made another double sub: Hincapie and Eze replace Tzolis and Calafiori, so all change down the left flank. For Hull, Lucas Herrington has replaced the injured Semi Ajayi at the back.

Felt like the cheers for Viktor Gyokeres to replace Kai Havertz were as much a reflection on frustrations with the German as enthusiasm for the Swede. Havertz has struggled today and is far less convincing in this sort of match – when the onus is more on the Arsenal to create – than he was in scoring the winner at Anfield last Sunday.

Specific explanation for Declan Rice’s substitution is unclear – he didn’t look injured – and so perhaps just reflection of risks associated with a third 90 minutes in six days alongside an acknowledgement of quality alternatives on the bench.

Some changes at the Emirates: Cho and Lewie Coyle are replaced by Joe Gelhardt and Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

It has been all Newcastle at the start of the second half and Harvey Barnes has now failed to take a hat-trick of chances. This was the best of the lot, running on to the ball, middle of the area from a perfectly weighted Yoane Wissa pass, he blasted a shot the wrong side of the post.

The second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

While Kai Havertz was in an offside position when his shirt was pulled, he may not have been active.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

However, the Premier League match centre does not see it that way.

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Frustrating first half for Arsenal, but it was never going to be easy to go again in the Premier League following a Champions League away game and last Sunday’s big win against Liverpool. Hull have also played with confidence and resolve.

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

I’ve spotted something else since I was covering Arsenal in 2018. I was gazing up at the boards that circle the top tier where the club mark every trophy that the team has won. There was previously this big gap, of course, from 2005 until 2014 before the cabinet gradually began refilling. But someone has since had a good idea. They have added all the women’s trophies as well, transforming the tally by just the odd 17 during those tricky years of transition and billionaire rivals owners in the men’s game.

Declan Rice has also just had a shot flash wide, but still no clear chances for either team.

Dan Burn thought he had scored from close-range, but Wissa has been penalised for blocking Castagne so the goal was ruled out.

#FULNEW – 33' The referee's call of no goal to Newcastle United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Wissa fouled Castagne in the build-up. AR2: "Defensive foul at the back post. Wissa holding at the back post". REF: "Castagne held back by Wissa. It's a deliberate foul". VAR: "He's clearly holding him - confirming the on-field decision of defensive free-kick. Wissa is clearly making an attempt to hold the Fulham defender. Clear holding offence".

Some controversy here as Newcastle appear to have had a perfectly good goal ruled out for an innocuous looking foul from Yoane Wissa on Timothy Costagne inside the box. Dan Burn was the scorer. Newcastle’s bench are furious. Most of us are just bemused.

Arsenal have largely been on top after Hull’s lively start but clear chances are scarce and Hull’s fans certainly sound increasingly confident. “You’re only here for the Tigers”, they say. To which a rendition of “champions” rings out. On that note, they had a replica of the Premier League trophy outside the Emirates before the match, with fans queuing up to get their photo with it.

The bright start from the visitors has not been maintained and Fulham have been on top for the last few minutes. Lukasz Hornicek just made a full-stretch save to deny Oscar Bobb and there is a sense inside the stadium that the first goal is coming.

Newcastle, as we have seen all too often recently, really struggle to pass through the lines and when the ball makes it out wide it invariably seems to go backwards again.

Although Harvey Barnes has just forced a good save from Leno from a Jacob Murphy cross. It was easily Newcastle’s best move of the match as Wissa and Osula linked up for the first time through the middle.

David Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Kai Havertz was going away from goal but Nobel Medy hardly subtle with his challenge – arm and leg – on the edge of the area. It would have been what we call soft but the sort of innocuous challenge that very often results in a foul elsewhere on the pitch.

On a self-indulgent note, this is an all-too-rare trip to the Emirates for me. I covered Arsenal for the last decade of the Arsene Wenger era, ending in 2018 and haven’t made many visits since. A few things are already striking: so many familiar faces still among the staff at a club that has always had more of a family feel than most. Outside, and few of the gaps in the middle (or top tier) that became evident during the final Wenger years when many fans clearly lost faith in the team’s title-winning credentials. The atmosphere is a notch up too.

Thiaw heads wide after a well-worked short corner from Newcastle, but the flag is up for offside in any case. Lewis Hall with the cross.

A decent start from Newcastle United against Fulham and you can see clearer patterns of play emerging. The fact that Fulham are constantly looking to build their attacks by playing out from the back has also helped. The home side have had a couple of scares already.

Hull gain some territory in the early exchanges, and win a corner via a long throw. From the set-piece, Egan’s set-piece hit the side-netting. A shot across Arsenal’s bows.

The lack of Mohamed Beloloumi’s creative spark clearly a big blow for Hull against the best defence in the league; a defence that will be further strengthened by the imminent return of William Saliba. Mikel Arteta had decided that Saliba would be better served by playing against Aston Villa for the Under-21s at Boreham Wood tomorrow. Hull have started on the front, though, in the opening minutes

Updates to follow from the Emirates and Craven Cottage. The Last Post was played and there was a minute’s silence as both grounds mark Remembrance Day.

It’s always great to be back home. It’s the last game before the international break so we know the importance of that and the challenges Hull will provide today. We’re super focused, it’s a massive game for us.

With the amount of games we’re playing, we need that freshness. The team has been performing really well, the finishers have been key again and that’s what we have today – start the game really, really strong and if we need to, have the ability to change the game.

Arsenal’s manager says the centre-back will play an Under-21s game tomorrow as the continues his recovery from a back injury.

Arteta says: “In regards to Willy as well, he needs some minutes. Obviously, the Champions League allows you to bring more players into the bench, but we believe that it’s the best thing to do: to play some minutes at the weekend with the Under-21s and then be fully fit for the international break.”

Arsenal are playing very good football, no matter Champions League or Premier League. They are very strong, they control everything not just against us, also other better clubs. But in football, we have a chance. Obviously, they are a big favourite, and we can start to try to create some difficulties for them.

The return of Sean Steur is a positive move from Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle but is it also a sign the German is feeling the pressure of public opinion on Tyneside?

The 18-year-old has looked the best of Newcastle’s summer signings but Newcastle are understandably trying to ease the teenager into things.

Ultimately, though, Steur is the only midfield player who can take possession of the ball under pressure and despite his tender years they have looked a better side with him in it.

There have been widespread calls for Steur to be called back into the side and Jaissle has done just that for a game he could really do with winning coming off the back of four defeats in their last five games.

Malick Thiaw also comes back into the side for Fabian Schar, with Jacob Murphy preferred to Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa starting in place of Joe Willock. I don’t think any of those dropped can have any complaints.

However, the constant chopping and changing betrays the problems Jaissle is facing. Whatever team he sends out is struggling to deliver what he wants, both individually and collectively.

With the international break coming up, Newcastle need a positive result to quieten the negative noise.

Fulham XI: Leno; Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson; Berge, Charles; Bobb, King, Iwobi; Garcia

Subs: Lecomte, Tete, Andersen, Palacios, Muniz, Kevin, Larsson, Angel, Sessegnon

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw, Burn, Hall; Steur, Gonzalez; Murphy, Wissa, Barnes; Osula

Subs: Pope, Livramento, Botman, Schar, Toure, Elanga, Fernandez-Pardo, Willock, Miley

A big blow for Hull to be without their most inventive and dangerous attacking player. It looks like Sergej Jakirovic has switched things up with a 5-3-2, and it will be a back five not a three for long periods.

Hull XI: Tzolakis, Coyle, Ajayi, Egan, Mendy, Stroud, Slater, Iroegbunam, Gourna, McBurnie, Cho

Subs: Butland, Giles, Thomas, Gelhardt, Hjerto-Dahl, Norton-Cuffy, Herrington, Mouzakitis, Vaz

Your Tigers to face Arsenal 👊 https://t.co/1kB7SbPA8Y

No William Saliba in the squad despite his inclusion in the Champions League, although you are allowed more subs on the bench in that competition. Otherwise, Arsenal as expected with Arteta deciding against picking a team without Rice.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard; Madueke, Havertz, Tzolis

Subs: Kepa, White, Mosquera, Hincapie, Lewis-Skelly, Zubimendi, Merino, Eze Gyokeres

🔴 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 ⚪️ Let's get it, Gunners 👊 🤝 @deel

Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal are “looking after” Declan Rice more now than in any previous campaign and has rejected suggestions that the England midfielder is being overplayed.

Rice played through nerve pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season, when he made an extraordinary 69 appearances for club and country.

The 27-year-old has played at least 60 matches in each of the past four campaigns, prompting concerns among Arsenal supporters that he is at risk of burnout or injury.

Arteta kept Rice on the field for the full 90 minutes of Arsenal’s midweek victory over Slavia Prague but insisted the club is working harder than ever to manage the midfielder’s workload.

So far this season, Rice has been left out of Arsenal’s two Carabao Cup matches and also withdrew from the previous international break in September.

Asked if he was concerned about Rice’s fitness, Arteta said: “Concerns? Which is the only player, the only player in this squad, that for two games in the Carabao Cup has been left out of the squad? At home with two days off? It’s not true [that Rice is being overplayed].

“We are really looking after him more than any other season. The way he is training and all the love [he is being shown]. That’s it.

“Here are the demands of this football club and a player like him. Not only him, because there are many others that have even less time. That’s it. That has to be the mindset. If you start to put other things in your brain, [it will create] damage. Erase them, get them in the bin and just focus on what you have to do.”

Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.

#1039. Man City appeal outcome over Premier League rules breach 'cannot leave room for doubt', says integrity chief

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules in September but have since lodged an appeal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Supporters must show patience over the Manchester City appeal outcome because it "cannot leave room for doubt", a sport integrity chief said.

An independent commission found the club guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations over nine seasons when it published its findings on 29 September.

The panel concluded City deliberately broke rules by inflating revenue or lowering costs by over £900million through "sham" arrangements to circumvent financial rules.

City’s appeal means the top-flight season continues without a final verdict or clarity over potential sanctions.

While this has raised questions over on-pitch integrity, Emanuel Macedo de Medeiros, co-founder and global chief executive of Sport Integrity Global Alliance (SIGA), insisted justice must come first.

"I understand the fans’ frustration, and I understand also the fans’ anguish, especially those who follow and support Manchester City," he told the Press Association.

"This is not a pleasant situation for anybody, but the law is the law, and it must be served on its own time, without constraints.

"Being a lawyer, I know that justice sometimes is served slowly. That is not because those who are in charge of the procedures are lazy, or they neglect their duties. It’s because there cannot be room for doubt. There cannot be room for failure.

"There cannot be any breach of the constitutional rights that those who are being scrutinised or judged enjoy. But I think it’s fair to say that the process is coming to an end."

Medeiros, speaking during Sport Integrity Action Month, stressed the importance of the case.

"This is also a test, not just for the Premier League and the credibility of the whole system, it is a test for the entirety of European football," he said. “It has involved rivers of ink and hours and hours of public debate. It is a matter of utmost interest for the football community.

"But there are no reasons for speculating regarding due process, and I’m pretty sure that the case will be finished sooner rather than later. Justice is served when it is served on the right time, and I think everyone is aware of that and conscious about their responsibilities."

The commission found City ran a "disguised funding scheme" where Abu Dhabi firms paid only a fraction of recorded sums, with Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), Sheikh Mansour’s ownership vehicle, settling the balance.

That arrangement inflated revenues by over £830m between 2009-10 and 2017-18. City also overstated image rights income by nearly £74m and understated staff contract liabilities by almost £17m.

City claimed the verdict featured "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

City chief executive Ferran Soriano told staff via video that the panel accepted the Premier League’s "conspiracy theory".

Kevin De Bruyne to Everton is on, with the Manchester City legend struggling at Napoli

Everton have launched a shock bid for former Manchester City man, Kevin De Bruyne.

The Belgian is a legend of the Premier League, having won six titles and racked up an in while racking up almost 200 goal involvements in 288 appearances in the English top flight – but since leaving the Etihad, things haven't been as rosy for him in Italian football.

Now, Everton are prepared to offer the 35-year-old a return to the northwest of England in one of the biggest-name moves of the Toffees' recent history.

De Bruyne spent 10 years at Manchester City before swapping one blue shirt for another and signing for Napoli last summer.

The playmaker has struggled to make a difference in Serie A, however, with Calciomercato reporting that he “appears to be in a decline mentally and could sensationally return to the Premier League in January.”

The report notes that Everton are making a sensational swoop to bring De Bruyne back to England and have already made contact with the player's entourage.

The Merseysiders are up to sixth in the Premier League at the moment and enjoying a good season, despite leaving themselves short over the summer in terms of transfer business.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Fans were disappointed when the club sold striker Beto without a replacement – leaving Thierno Barry as the only recognised No.9 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium – while a failure to replace long-serving right-back Seamus Coleman after his retirement has meant that midfielder Merlin Rohl has taken the role on this term.

There has been recent uncertainty regarding the loan spell of Jack Grealish, too, with the England international dropped by manager David Moyes after breaching the club's disciplinary rules when he reportedly skipped training.

Grealish – who is on loan from Man City, incidentally – has very little chance of joining the Toffees permanently now, with some suggesting that his loan spell could be curtailed in January.

De Bruyne's contract runs until 2027, with the Partenopei holding an option for another year.

Whether club president Aurelio De Laurentiis decides to release the player midseason remains another matter.

The 35-year-old is worth €8 million, as per Transfermarkt. Everton travel away to Brentford when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Knockout spots, relegation dogfights, and crucial seeding: why this week's Nations League action matters far more than you think

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forget the notion of glorified friendlies, this month quarter-final berths, relegation peril, and major tournament seeding is all on the line in the UEFA Nations League.

The final round of group fixtures is anything but an international break distraction.

Here, we break down what it all means for the home nations.

The top two finishers in each League A group advance to a two-legged quarter-final stage, rather than just the group winners qualifying directly for a final-four tournament, as has previously been the case.

This week’s fixtures decide which nations book their place in the knockout bracket to compete for the trophy, while also dictating important top-seed status for the subsequent knockout draw.

The margins between tiers carry significant weight. Finishing top of the group in Leagues B, C, and D earns automatic promotion to the tier above, while finishing bottom of Leagues A, B, and C results in automatic relegation.

Crucially, the introduction of two-legged promotion/relegation play-offs - which will pit third-placed teams in League A against runners-up from League B, and third-placed teams in League B against runners-up from League C - means almost every matchday result directly determines either immediate survival, a climb up the ladder, or a drop into lower-tier fixtures.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Nations League standings double as an insurance policy for future European Championship and FIFA World Cup cycles.

Overall tournament rankings determine the seeding pots for upcoming European qualifying draws, directly affecting the difficulty of qualification paths. The highest-ranked Nations League group winners who fail to secure qualification through standard qualifying groups are handed secondary lifelines via tournament play-off berths.

England currently sit second in their group with nine points, trailing Spain (12 points) but comfortably ahead of Croatia (3 points) and Czechia (0 points).

Because the top two teams in League A advance, Thomas Tuchel's side have already effectively secured their quarter-final berth. The focus now shifts to whether they can overtake Spain for the group's top seed.

Thursday, Nov 12: vs Croatia (H – Wembley Stadium, London) - 19:45 GMT

Sunday, Nov 15: vs Spain (A – Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid) - 19:45 GMT

Wales are third in their top-tier group, trailing Portugal and Denmark, but sitting just above Norway. To avoid a relegation play-off against a League B runner-up or automatic relegation if they drop to fourth, they need results this week to either secure their safety or mount a late push into the top two for a quarter-final spot.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Norway (A – Ullevaal Stadium, Oslo) - 17:00 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Portugal (H – Cardiff City Stadium, Cardiff) - 19:45 GMT

Scotland find themselves in third place behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with North Macedonia rooted to the bottom. Finishing third in League B leads to a relegation play-off against a League C side, so the Tartan Army will be keen to pick up points and push for second place (promotion play-off) or even top spot (automatic promotion).

Friday, Nov 13: vs North Macedonia (H – Hampden Park, Glasgow) - 19:45 GMT

Monday, Nov 16: vs Switzerland (A – Kybunpark, St. Gallen) - 19:45 GMT

Michael O'Neill's side are in an excellent position, currently top of their group ahead of Hungary, Ukraine, and Georgia. If they maintain their first-place standing over the next two games, they will earn automatic promotion to League A.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Ukraine (H – Windsor Park, Belfast) - 19:45 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Hungary (A – Puskas Arena, Budapest) - 19:45 GMT

The Republic of Ireland sit in third on five points, trailing group leaders Austria and second-placed Kosovo. They will need strong performances in this window to climb into the top two for a shot at promotion, or risk facing a relegation play-off to retain their League B status.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Austria (A – Raiffeisen Arena, Linz) - 19:45 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Kosovo (H – Aviva Stadium, Dublin) - 19:45 GMT

#1036. Next Man United manager: Who could replace Michael Carrick?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick is on the brink after another chaotic performance in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, which leaves United stuck in the bottom three during the international break

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick appears to be on the brink of being sacked by Manchester United, with the club inside the relegation zone during the international break and considering a fourth permanent manager in three years since minority owners Ineos, under Sir Jim Ratcliffe, took control of football operations.

Carrick – who impressed during his interim spell in charge last season – has seen the goodwill this season evaporate after United’s worst start to a season in 40 years, with a disastrous defensive performance seeing them go two goals down against Aston Villa before a miraculous late comeback earned a 4-4 draw.

Liverpool away after the international break offers little hope of escaping the drop zone, before a trip to Lisbon in the Champions League.

While the problems United face run far deeper than the head coach – as highlighted by defender Lisandro Martinez after the defeat to Atletico Madrid earlier this month – while criticism of Carrick’s tactics came from United captain Bruno Fernandes, who has not been able to inspire the team in the manner that saw him pick up the PFA Player of the Year award and the league’s assist record last term.

So if United do finally pull the trigger on another change of manager, who could be in charge at Anfield and beyond in a bid to, firstly, guide the club away from a relegation battle?

The current odds-on favourite after emerging as a key target, yet Man United could face a problem getting the Argentine out of his United States contract, having committed to terms up to the next World Cup in 2030. Compensation in excess of £7m could follow, yet United are in a desperate situation and the experience and presence of Pochettino could spark a reaction from a group desperately short of inspiration. Pochettino’s powers have waned since his famous spell with Spurs, though his exit at Chelsea came at the end of a promising run to conclude the 2023/24 season. There was immense potential and excitement to start the 2026 World Cup, but a combination of the Folarin Balogun scandal and then a thumping at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 took the shine off Pochettino’s performance from the dugout. Now, it remains to be seen if he can deliver once more in club football in what would surely be his most difficult job to date.

The Englishman is available after his shock decision to leave Newcastle United in the summer. Howe told the club he needed a break from management but the chance to take charge at Old Trafford, three months later, would surely be too good to turn down if an offer arrives. The 48-year-old remains highly regarded in English football after taking over a Newcastle side in the relegation zone and leading them to the club’s highest Premier League finish in two decades, as well as their first domestic silverware in 70 years. Howe twice took Newcastle into the Champions League playing an energetic, high-intensity style of football that would be popular at Old Trafford. He is currently the favourite with the bookies.

Brighton have been the surprise package in the Premier League this season and the 33-year-old Hurzeler has drawn praise for turning the Seagulls into a side capable of competing with the country’s biggest clubs. Brighton’s 3-0 victory over champions Arsenal earlier this season was a masterclass in modern coaching while Hurzeler’s side also knocked United out of the Carabao Cup with a brilliant 3-2 win at Old Trafford. The Independent’s Chief Football Writer Miguel Delaney has reported that Hurzeler is admired at Old Trafford but Brighton would demand significant compensation for the highly-rated German and United may not have the cash. At Brighton, Hurzeler has also enjoyed an environment where the club have made all the right decisions off the pitch. At United, he would arguably be walking into the opposite.

The Brighton boss said on Friday: “I’m fully focused on my job here. I’ve got no time to think about these rumours because we play every three days. I have a lot of respect for Michael Carrick and the job he has done at Manchester United the last season. He's a great human being, a great personality, and I really respect him. There's nothing more to say about that. I’m really privileged to be here. I’m part of a journey [at Brighton] and I still have this feeling when I go to bed that we are not finished with our journey... “We have built this [together] over the years. We’ve had good periods, we’ve had bad periods. To build these connections you need time. You don’t take these things for granted. It’s a people business. Making a people business out of this pressure business is something I don’t take for granted and something I won’t throw away that fast.”

The former wunderkind of German coaching was reportedly on United’s radar when they sacked Ruben Amorim at the start of the year, but as an option for the summer following the World Cup. Well, that was a bit of a disaster for the former Bayern Munich and RB Leipzig coach, as Germany were knocked out in the last-32 by Paraguay. Nagelsmann, 39, would naturally be interested in managing United and the club’s director of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, previously worked with him at Red Bull.

The Spaniard has done a superb job at Aston Villa by securing Champions League qualification and ending the club’s trophy drought with victory in the Europa League. But Aston Villa will be even more determined to keep Emery given the club are only in the early stages of their rebuild under him, having completely overhauled the spine of their team over the summer. As it is, Emery enjoys complete control over his project at Villa Park, a reality he is unlikely to find at Old Trafford, while he appears enthused by the challenge of constructing a second competitive team in the Premier League. With Emery, who is under contract until 2029, United would also need to pay Villa compensation, and that may place him above their budget.

The appeal of the combustible Italian only has grown while United have been accused of becoming too passive and pedestrian on the pitch. Conte is one of the most demanding coaches in the game and would instantly bring a level of intensity and urgency that has been lacking this season, while his CV – with Serie A titles at Juventus, Inter Milan and Napoli and a Premier League crown with Chelsea – commands respect. Conte also brought an immediate improvement when he took charge of a floundering Tottenham five years ago and led them back into the Champions League, which now has to be United’s biggest concern. So the 57-year-old offers impact, but then what? Conte has a sharp tongue and is not afraid to criticise his bosses if he feels they are failing to support him. His exit from Tottenham in March 2023 followed a stunning evisceration of the club in a now legendary press conference at Southampton. United would be playing with fire but options of Conte’s calibre are few and far between.

In a statement on Friday, Conte distanced himself from the Manchester United job while branding reports that he is in “advanced negotiations” with any club as “speculation”. He said: “Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right. I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my ‘strong personality’. These reports are unfounded, as there is currently no concrete basis for such assessments.”

The former Arsenal, Barcelona and Chelsea midfielder is developing a reputation as Europe’s brightest young coach – as his brilliant Como side demonstrated by thrashing United in the Champions League on Wednesday night. The Spaniard appears committed to his project in northern Italy, though, and also has a financial incentive to continue leading Como in their debut Champions League campaign due to owning a stake in the Serie A club. The 39-year-old’s own stock is also rising and the lure of returning to one of his former clubs in the future, such as Barcelona, could result in Fabregas taking a patient and considered approach to his next move.

Well, we’ve been here before. It was Under-18s manager Darren Fletcher, who oversaw the draw with Burnley and FA Cup third-round defeat to Brighton, before Michael Carrick stepped into the breach in January. Before him, Ruud van Nistelrooy held the reins between Erik ten Hag’s dismissal and Amorim’s appointment and before that, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer experienced the same cycle of boom-and-bust that Carrick has gone through over the past 10 months. In short, there are numerous former United players who are available to remind an underperforming dressing room of the importance of the badge and the meaning of the shirt. It could be time for Fletcher to give Sir Alex another call.

Manchester City’s feud with the Premier League following the guilty verdict will dominate their season, but it is now events on the pitch that are proving a genuine concern.

Enzo Maresca has lost three league games in a row and, at the City Ground, there was further evidence of defensive instability, strange team selection and key players underperforming.

Eight games without a clean sheet underlines their vulnerability and Maresca has much to ponder over the international break with his team six points behind leaders Arsenal.

What a response from Nottingham Forest to Oliver Glasner’s brutal “no-compromises” rant last weekend, as the home team secured only the second league win in front of their own supporters this year.

It was a former City player, Liam Delap, who tormented them with two brilliant individual goals to give Glasner what he hopes will finally be lift-off.

Forest come into this evening’s game in 19th, but they are just a point behind Crystal Palace and Manchester United, while victory would also take them above Coventry City and up to 16th.

Forest’s results at the City Ground have to improve quickly or this team will be in serious trouble.

They have gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

The Manchester United hierarchy must not disregard relegation as an impossibility after one win in their opening 10 league matches this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox are scheduled to sit down with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco this week.

Head coach Michael Carrick’s future is expected to dominate the agenda at the pre-planned meeting in the principality where Ratcliffe is based. There is every chance a far more unpalatable subject will also be confronted given Man United's start to the 2026/27 season: drafting a contingency plan for relegation.

Ten games into the Premier League campaign, Man United find themselves in the bottom three with just a solitary victory. Minority owners INEOS arrived at Old Trafford boasting elite operating standards and a clear structure but on the pitch, the team has been dragged into a survival scrap for the second year running.

Acknowledging the drop remains something of a taboo for a club of Man United's size and commercial footprint, but a recent warning from north London shows why ignoring it would constitute negligence.

Speaking on The Sports Agents podcast, Tottenham Hotspur chief executive Vinai Venkatesham revealed how the club were planning for the future after Spurs flirted with disaster last season.

“It's really tough, because you form a relationship with people. Obviously, Igor [Tudor] wasn't the coach for long, but Thomas [Frank], we worked together really, really, really closely, went through some really difficult times," Venkatesham explained.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Spurs ultimately secured survival on the final day, but Venkatesham admitted the club had quietly mapped out a blueprint for the Championship.

“It was really challenging. A really, really, really challenging period for the club,” he said. “You have to [prepare for relegation]. I mean, you can't not. To not make that plan would have been irresponsible… Sometimes going through something as traumatic as what we went through last season bonds people a little bit and also puts even more fire in everybody's belly to make sure that something like that can never happen again.”

That brush with the drop motivated Spurs to spend £300 million on summer transfer targets, including £100m on Newcastle United's Sandro Tonali and £85m on West Ham United midfielder Matheus Fernandes.

“Everybody was aligned we wanted to strengthen this position, and then everybody was aligned that Matheus [Fernandes] was absolutely the number one target,” Venkatesham said. “If I'm honest, we achieved more than we thought we might do, and that was really because so many of our number one targets we were able to land. Because if we weren't going to get our number one targets, we weren't going to settle.”

Even with morale lifted by recent wins, Venkatesham reflected honestly on their sluggish start: “I wasn't worried [by the start to the 2026/27 season], but I was definitely frustrated… Did we think we were going to make this many changes and everything would gel straight away? Of course we didn't. But did we think we'd be hovering around the position of the league that we were in the international break? Of course we didn't either.”

For Ratcliffe, Berrada, and Wilcox, Venkatesham’s transparency should rid them of any lingering delusions of grandeur. Precedent proves that stature, revenue, and history offer little insulation once a club slips into the bottom three.

Whether Man United decide to back Carrick through the November break or sack him, the decision-making trio at the Monaco summit cannot afford to treat the drop as an unthinkable scenario.

That might mean re-thinking squad wage-reduction clauses or auditing broadcast revenue drop-offs, because after all, responsible governance demands preparing for the worst.

If Man United pretend they are simply too big to go down, that is the quickest way to end up there.

#1032. Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Minimalist biotechnology companies that have just a handful of employees — or even as few as one — are becoming more feasible with the rise of artificial-intelligence tools.Credit: Getty

How many scientists does it take to discover a drug?

The question came to the fore after news that a biotechnology company armed with an artificial-intelligence assistant, two promising drug leads and just one full-time human employee had been acquired by San Francisco-based Anthropic as part of the AI giant’s expansion into biomedical science.

AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

In truth, it took many human scientists to develop the molecules that are the mini-company’s star products: two antibodies that are still in the early stages of development and were designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy. The company, Mithril Medicine in Cambridge, Massachusetts, also hired part-time consultants to advise on the project, and paid at least five contract research organizations to conduct experiments. Many more researchers will be needed to carry the drug further, especially if it eventually enters clinical trials. “It takes a village to develop a drug,” says Jeb Keiper, a partner at Third Rock Ventures, a venture-capital firm in Boston, Massachusetts.

But the news sparked a wave of discussions about whether the one-person biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future. “We will see more and more of these small teams that are enabled by AI,” says James Zou, a computer scientist who works on biomedical applications of AI at Stanford University in California. “They will be very powerful for identifying good opportunities and moving quickly.”

Itsy-bitsy biotechs are not a new concept. Entrepreneur Matt Davidson started his first biotech company in 2013, nearly a decade before ChatGPT’s public debut. Davidson kept the roster trim for years, with only two full-time employees until the drug he was developing was ready to enter late-stage clinical testing. The company never had a physical laboratory, Davidson says. All the lab work was contracted out.

His current company, Azora Therapeutics in Los Angeles, California, has a whopping five employees. He uses AI more for summarizing reports than for scientific discovery and says that AI tools have made tiny biotechs more efficient. “We use consultants a little bit less than we used to,” he says.

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Mithril Medicine leaned more heavily on AI than Azora does, and tasked Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude with helping to analyse data and suggesting next steps, as well as taming the piles of emails and paperwork that come from working with multiple contract research organizations. “What began as an exercise in staying lean evolved into the thesis for an entirely new operating model, which we now call Pipeline-in-a-Person,” wrote Cody Tranbarger, Mithril’s former chief executive and lone employee, on LinkedIn. (Tranbarger, who works for Anthropic since Mithril was absorbed into it, declined to speak to Nature, as did Anthropic.)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03640-9

The legendary Scottish manager hailed Mauricio Pochettino back in 2016, with the Argentine strongly linked a decade on to succeed Michael Carrick after a dismal run of form for United

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United could finally hire Mauricio Pochettino a decade after Sir Alex Ferguson endorsed the Argentine manager due to his commitment to young players.

The United States boss is the favourite to succeed Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, should Ineos and the Glazer family sanction a change in the dugout following a Monaco summit.

After a disastrous start to the season, United sit inside the relegation zone, but despite immense pressure, Carrick took training on Wednesday morning.

And with the United hierarchy meeting on Wednesday to make a final call on Carrick, Pochettino is currently the favourite to be the next manager at Old Trafford, with Ferguson’s appreciation of the former Tottenham and Chelsea boss longstanding.

"Well the manager has been fantastic," the Scot said back in 2016, with Pochettino then linked with the job several times since 2018.

"They have a bad record of managers, there is no doubt about that. They have had so many over the years, but this lad has composure.

"You never see him ruffled and the way his team play is a testimony to the work he is doing.

"The most important thing for English football is how many English and young players are in his team.

"He understands the advantage of playing young people. They won't let you down and they have been fantastic."

Pochettino previously met Ferguson for lunch in London and have had a friendly relationship since their time at League Managers Association dinners.

Should United opt for a change, compensation would be due to the United States federation, with Pochettino recently signing a new deal to take him up to the 2030 World Cup.

#1030. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

Jorgen Strand Larsen thought he had the opener against Liverpool, but it was ruled out for offside! ❌ https://t.co/JkSKbtkvak

The other factor which seems likely to condemn Sage is his team’s boneheaded defensive lapses. Liverpool were awarded a debatable free-kick out wide, Quinten Timber let Mac Allister run off him too easily and he duly nodded Dominik Szoboszlai’s delivery past Dean Henderson with ease. Another header conceded.

Liverpool have taken the lead against Crystal Palace thanks to Alexis Mac Alister's header! 💥 https://t.co/kNal7qsQ35

Mac Allister, formerly of Brighton, endeared himself to the Holmesdale Road Stand with a priggish celebration. There was some blowback from the seats closest, but a more dominant sense of resignation. Someone in the adjoining block took out their phone and snapped a picture. Formerly hated rival scoring against you, rubbing it in with his celebration: truly one to show the grandkids.

Liverpool had put together little of substance until then, with Wirtz drifting through another half, Alexander Isak looking keen but flawed and Barcola spooning a promising shot into low-Earth orbit. The second half was better, but Isak looked to have wasted his best chance, a one-on-one with Henderson thumped too close to the goalkeeper.

Isak had his moment in the end, checking back to finish calmly at the end of a counter-attack against a tiring defence. Eight for the season for him and an assist for Wirtz, too, although it was hardly a pass of Molbyesque majesty.

“Happy for him,” Iraola said of Wirtz, also praising Isak’s movement for the German’s goal. “I think [Wirtz] has been very unlucky in the Premier League, a couple of goals disallowed and situations where he deserves honestly to score.”

So it was Liverpool’s blip righted here, despite all of Palace’s pressure. Alisson, who took some flak for his performance at Fenerbahce, was hard to fault. He may not have reached Eddie Nketiah’s stoppage-time penalty, but made a series of brave saves and deserved a clean sheet. For all that attacking talent, the long-serving goalkeeper still looks like one of Iraola’s most important players.

13 - Liverpool have earned more points away from home in the Premier League this season than any other side (13). It's the Reds' joint-most ever from their first five away matches of a league campaign. Journeymen. https://t.co/lFe8MO3T6m

"We were efficient in front of goal" Florian Wirtz was happy with Liverpool's attacking display against Crystal Palace ⚽️ https://t.co/E0U2UJiiao

FULL TIME: Brighton's fine start to the season continues after a comfortable win against ten player Brentford, Florian Wirtz bags his first goal of the season as Liverpool inflict more pain on Crystal Palace, Bournemouth edge past Ipswich at Portman Road to continue their fine form and Sunderland pick up a huge win at home to Chelsea!

Liverpool condemn Palace to a fourth successive Premier League defeat. Mac Allister, Wirtz and Isak were all on target for the visitors, before Nketiah netted a last-gasp penalty. This result leaves Palace rooted to the bottom of the table following Sunderland’s win over Chelsea, while Liverpool move up to fourth. Will this end up being Sage’s last game in charge of Palace?

Finally, Alisson is beaten. Nketiah steps up and slams a confident penalty into the net. The Liverpool goalkeeper dives the correct way, but can’t keep it out as his clean sheet disappears. Palace’s attacking efforts have deserved a goal.

There’s a clash of heads in Liverpool’s penalty area as Kerkez and Osorio both challenge for the ball. The Hungarian catches the Palace attacker and he’s late, so the referee points to the spot.

Following that goal, Isak is withdrawn and replaced by Koumas. There’s four minutes of added time to end this game.

A good day but a middling performance from Liverpool. A goal for Wirtz, an assist for Barcola, and now Isak doing his bit for the revival narrative. Contributions from three of the most criticised members of Liverpool’s expensively-assembled attacking group. Not sure we will be seeing a great deal more of Pierre Sage in the Selhurst Park dugout.

Game, set and match for Liverpool. The visitors break as Munoz whips a cross into Wirtz, who has the composure to play in Isak. The striker cuts inside of a desperate challenge before smashing a clinical, close-range effort into the roof of the net. Palace fans flood out of Selhurst Park. Sage cuts a dejected figure on the sidelines.

"Isak's a Red, ole ole..." 🎶 https://t.co/ME0QB7Km48

Henderson makes a goal-saving stop. Mitchell fails to deal with a high clearance and Munoz pounces on the mistake before teeing up Isak. The Liverpool striker is through on goal, but Henderson does brilliantly to block his one-on-one effort. Sage makes a late double change as Khalaili and McNeil replace Mingueza and Pino.

Wirtz tests Henderson with a whipped attempt following Nyoni’s strong run and Munoz’s lay-off. However, the Palace captain makes a simple save.

Munoz tries to dribble away from Lerma, but the Liverpool substitute dives over the Palace man’s outstretched leg. Mac Allister then unnecessarily squares up to Lerma because of his annoyed reaction to Munoz’s simulation. As a result, all three of the aforementioned players are booked.

Palace can’t find a way past Alisson. Osorio drives down the wing and picks out the unmarked Pino, whose shot is smothered by the Liverpool goalkeeper. Lerma latches onto the loose ball, but Alisson is there once again to comfortably gather the Palace man’s ambitious rebound.

Liverpool continue to protect their two-goal advantage and make another forward change as Ngumoha comes on for Gakpo.

Sage makes an attacking change as Nketiah, who scored the winner against Liverpool at Selhurst Park in September 2025, replaces Strand Larsen up top.

In fairness to Palace, you can’t fault their effort. Liverpool are holding firm and the hosts are lacking end-product. Pino then catches Araujo with a late tackle to pick up a needless booking.

No need to be dramatic, but this does rather feel like the season for Pierre Sage. Losing games you have created the best chances in is a bad look for a manager under pressure, especially in the specific circumstances Palace are displaying. There is enough promise and talent in his team to suggest a different voice could extract more from the group. There is also a dreadful habit of switching off entirely, which might make a chairman wonder if it is time for more of a shouty presence in the dugout. The second Liverpool goal was woeful from a Palace point of view.

Iraola makes a double change as Nyoni and Munoz replace Szoboszlai and Barcola.

Alisson claims Wharton’s cross as Strand Larsen falls on the Liverpool goalkeeper. The Brazilian has been faultless today and looks well on the way to a deserved clean sheet as things stand.

The game has become quite chaotic and Palace’s shape has deserted them. If there’s another goal in this game, then it will be absolutely crucial. The hosts are waiting to craft a notable second-half chance.

Sage makes a change on the hour-mark as Osorio replaces Timber in the game’s first alteration.

Barcola is booked after halting a Palace counter with a forceful challenge through the back of Pino.

That second Liverpool goal has left Selhurst Park very deflated. All the noise is coming from the away fans. Mitchell’s makes a crucial intervention to block Barcola’s cross. Palace look so stretched now.

It’s an excellent team goal as two of Liverpool’s big-money attackers devastatingly combine. Barcola is released down the wing and finds Wirtz with a low, pinpoint cross. The German playmaker then sweeps a composed, first-time effort into the bottom corner, leaving Henderson rooted to the spot. It’s a wonderful finish and credit to Barcola for the assist. Palace are in trouble and have a mountain to climb.

Timber slides a pass in behind Jacquet for Strand Larsen to chase. However, Alisson is alert to the danger and rushes off his line to collect possession.

We are back under way at Selhurst Park. Both sides are unchanged at the break. Can Palace find a way back into this contest?

A thoroughly entertaining first half at Selhurst Park comes to a close as Liverpool hold a slender 1-0 lead over Palace thanks to Mac Allister’s 40th-minute header. Palace struck the bar through Pino and had a Strand Larsen goal ruled out for offside, but Liverpool have also looked dangerous going forward and their opener came as no surprise to anyone. To Palace’s credit, they’ve really taken the game to Liverpool so far, forcing Alisson into a couple of notable saves. However, there was still boos at half-time and Sage has work to do.

Much fury and gnashing of teeth towards the referee Tony Harrington at half time. The tunnel entrance takes players and officials past some of Palace’s most vociferous fans and several were giving him their most strident opinions.

Anger mostly towards the free kick which led to the goal, but it didn’t seem too egregious a decision to me.

Score is very harsh on Palace, though with Kamada, Strand Larsen and Pino all coming desperately close. Exactly the sort of hard luck story you’d expect from a team in trouble.

We lead at the break 👊 #CRYLIV https://t.co/7e9WF0j1KA

Despite Szoboszlai’s enforced absence and Liverpool’s numerical disadvantage, Barcola leads an attack that creates a shooting opportunity for Wirtz, which is blocked by Disasi. Alisson produces another sensational stop. A teasing cross is glanced towards goal by Wharton, whose header is parried away by the diving Liverpool goalkeeper. Alisson has been in inspired form so far this afternoon.

Szoboszlai hangs a deep cross towards the back post. Gakpo directs it back across goal with a first-time volley, but no Liverpool has the attacking instinct to take a chance and anticipate it. Isak was instead loitering near the penalty spot. The visitors are well on top here.

Palace have been careless in possession so far, prompting groans from the home support. Szoboszlai draws a save from Henderson with a bobbling long-range strike, forcing the Palace captain into conceding a corner.

Liverpool are popping the ball around with real intent as Gakpo clips a teasing cross into Barcola. It’s just out of the winger’s reach, with Barcola claiming he was pushed by Mingueza. Fun start. Gets short shrift from the referee and Palace fans.

It’s been a fast-paced and frantic start to this game. Isak’s delightful touch takes him away from Disasi, who pulls the Liverpool forward to the ground, giving the visitors a free kick. The Palace defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a yellow card for that foul.

Mitchell lashes a dangerous delivery across the six-yard box towards Strand Larsen, but solid defensive work from Van Dijk and Araujo allow Liverpool to clear.

Barcola lofts a ball over the top of Palace’s backline for Isak to latch onto. However, Disasi recovers well and blocks the Liverpool striker’s fierce half-volley from a tight angle.

A loose pass at the back from Palace gifts Liverpool an early opportunity, but Henderson does well to get down low and gather Mac Allister’s low, fizzing effort from outside the penalty area.

Liverpool get us under way at Selhurst Park. Can Iraola inflict more misery on Sage?

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.
